defs_parts: Six labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow.
In the book text: the course text uses and explains the term.
In the glossary: the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it.
Editor or docs: the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation.
Computed: the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs.
Simulation: a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game.
Conceptual: a drawing of the idea, with no data behind it.
recap_lines: The Outliner lists Actors in the level, and the Content Browser lists assets.
A Blueprint class is the template, and each placed copy is an Actor.
Play In Editor makes you the player, and Simulate runs with no player.
Edits made to Actors during play are thrown away when you press Stop.
Dot u asset and dot u map files are binary, so text tools cannot merge them.
A collision pair gets the weaker of its two responses.

I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Wait for my answer before you give yours.

beats.narration_text: Two drawings of the same cube, from two cameras. Perspective shows depth, so far things look smaller. Orthographic drops depth, so parallel edges stay parallel and equal. Measured here, the short edge divided by the long edge is zero point six seven in perspective, and one point zero zero in orthographic. Perspective is the default view. For example, to line up a row of platforms at exactly one height, you would switch to an orthographic Side view.

beats.narration_text: Now three view modes. A view mode is a way of drawing the same scene, such as Lit, Unlit and Wireframe. Lit shades each face by the light, here from a grey of one hundred twenty to two hundred forty. Unlit gives every face the same grey. Wireframe draws only the twelve edges. The scene itself never changes. For example, if a dark corner of your level hides a coin, switch to Unlit to see that the coin is really there.
